title: The Judgment Comes Home to Israel
overview: Amos finishes his charges against Israel's neighbors and then turns the same verdict on Judah and, at greatest length, on Israel itself for crushing its own poor.

parts.label: Moab's crime (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The pattern of three sins and then a fourth is a set phrase, and scholars debate whether it means sins piled up past counting or points to the final crime that is then named. Moab is condemned for burning an enemy king's bones to powder, a deep insult to the dead in that world, and its chief city Kerioth and its leaders will fall in war.

parts.label: Judah's crime (vv. 4-5)
parts.note: The neighbors were charged with cruelty to people, but Judah is charged with throwing away God's law and following false gods, as earlier generations had. Jerusalem's fortresses were later burned by the Babylonians.

parts.label: Israel's injustice (vv. 6-8)
parts.note: Israel, the northern kingdom and Amos's main audience, sells honest and poor people for money or something as cheap as a pair of sandals, whether through bribed courts or debt slavery, and grinds the powerless down. Men lounge at shrines on cloaks taken from the poor as loan security, which the law said must be returned by nightfall, and the girl shared by father and son may be a servant or a shrine prostitute, as scholars are unsure which.

parts.label: What God had done (vv. 9-10)
parts.note: The Amorites stand for the earlier peoples of Canaan, pictured as giants, whom the text says God destroyed root and branch so Israel could have the land, a claim many readers find troubling. The point Amos presses is ingratitude: a people freed from Egypt and given a home now treat their own poor as slaves.

parts.label: Silencing the messengers (vv. 11-12)
parts.note: Nazirites were people under a vow to avoid wine and leave their hair uncut, as a sign of being set apart for God. Israel pressured them to break their vows and told prophets to stop speaking, which is what an official later tells Amos himself in chapter 7.

parts.label: No one will escape (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: The image is of a cart overloaded with grain pressing down, though the exact Hebrew wording is uncertain. Even the fastest, strongest and bravest soldiers will fail and flee with nothing, and Israel did fall to Assyria in 722 BC.

think: Amos lists the crimes of other nations first and saves his sharpest words for his own people; why might wrongdoing be easier to see in outsiders than in one's own community?
